newsitem.title: CHINA: China, France in joint communique to build ties.
newsitem.headline: China, France in joint communique to build ties.

text.p: China and France pledged on Friday to a joint global partnership into the 21st century, issued a veiled message to the United States against world domination and urged a ban on fissile material for nuclear weapons.

"At the dawn of the 21st century, the time has come for France and China to prolong this initiative with a long term global partnership aimed at improving French-Chinese relations into a new phase of development," said a communique, signed by French President Jacques Chirac and China's Jiang Zemin.

The communique, clearly targeting superpower dominance by the United States, crowned Chirac's four-day state visit that opened on Thursday with a rallying cry to make Beijing a major political and business partner into the next century and was sealed by some $1.8 billion in contracts for French firms.

"The two parties have decided to engage in reinforced cooperation, to foster the march toward multipolarity... and to oppose any attempt at domination in world affairs," the communique said, citing areas of tension around the world.

President Jiang grinned with delight as he handed a poem in his calligraphy to Chirac, before signing the communique with the European head of state who has taken a lead in playing down criticism of China's human rights record and opposing a western move this year to censure Beijing in the United Nations.

Chirac gave the Chinese president and Communist Party chief a framed original French factory employment permit of his predecessor, the late paramount Deng Xiaoping, who worked in France in the early 1920s. Deng died, aged 92, on February 19.
Jiang also accepted an invitation to visit France.
The communique touched on human rights, with the two sides agreeing to take into account each others "particularities" and China praising Chirac's decision on U.N. criticism.
In talks on Thursday, Jiang described as a "wise decision" French opposition to censuring China over human rights.
France's Foreign Minister Herve de Charette was expected to raise individual human rights cases with China on Friday.

Speaking later at the National School of Administration of China, Chirac stressed the need for rule of law if China was to gain international trust and praised a new criminal code that alters the titles of political crimes.

In the communique, the world's last two powers to engage in nuclear testing voiced support for the global test ban and urged a swift start to talks on banning production of fissile material for nuclear weapons and other nuclear explosive devices.
One high level meeting between the two countries would be held each year with at least two meetings a year between their foreign ministers, it said.

The document also urged an expansion of the U.N. Security Council and stressed the importance of trade and investment, pledging to limit obstacles to market access and to boost cooperation in satellite construction and space research.
Chirac arrived on Thursday for a four-day state visit that has already seen the signing of more than $1.8 billion in business deals, mostly in the aviation sector.

Airbus Industrie won a $1.5 billion deal to sell 10 A320 and 20 A321 planes to Chinese airlines and signed an agreement to produce in China a 100-seat passenger jet that is expected to net around $40 billion in sales for the partners.

Sino-French relations soured in the early 1990s over sales of French jet fighters and frigates to China's rival, Taiwan, but have recovered since Paris pledged in 1994 to end arms sales to the island that Beijing considers a rebel province.

"The two parties express their conviction that the establishment of a global French-Chinese partnership will raise the traditional relations of friendship and cooperation that unite the two countries to a new level," the communique concluded.
